G Ood morrow my good Lord Chamberlaine.
speeches.Cham:: Many good morrowes to my good Lord of Sussex. Forward I pray.
speeches.Suss:: Whose with the Queene my Lord. A word my Lord in priuate. Good morrow Lords. Good morrow my Lord, good morrow good Sir Henry. The suffolke men my Lord, was to the Queene The very stayres, by which she did ascend: Shee's greatly bound vnto them for their loues. Your dutyes Lords. All forbeare this place vnlesse the Princesse. You shall not kneele where Sussex sits in place, The Chamber keeper, a chaire there for her grace. Madam he did not. The same day Frogmorton was arrain'd in the Guild-hall, It was impos'd on him, whether this Princesse had a hand With him or no; he did deny it, Cler'd her sore his death, yet accus'd others. Come my lords, lett's all ioyne in one peticion To the Queene, that she may not be lodg'd within the Tower. Now god forbid, a better hap heauen send: Thus men may mourne, for what they cannot mend. Exeunt omnes. Why doth the Princesse keepe her barge so longe, Why lands she not? Some one goe see the cause. Oh me my Lord, her state is wondrous hard, I haue seene the day, my hand Ide not haue lent To bring my Soueraignes Sister to the Tower: Good my Lords, stretch your Commission To doe this Princesse but some little fauour. Marry a God not I, no, no, not I; Yet who shall hinder these my eyes to sorrow For her sorrow: By Gods marry deere, That the Queene could not, though her selfe were here: My Lords, my Lords, if it were held fowle treason, To grieue for her hard vsage, by my Soule My eyes would hardly prooue me a true Subiect: But tis the Queenes pleasure, and we must obay: But I shall mourne, should the King and Queene say nay. Marry a God, tis true and tis no reason: Lanch Bargeman. Good Lady land, where Traitors vse to land, And fore her guilt be proou'd, Gods marry no, And the Queene wils it, that it should be so. As good a Lady as ere England bread, Would he that caus'd this woe, had lost his head. My Lord, you deale too cruelly with the Princesse, You knew her father, shee's no stranger to you. Good Lady take my cloake. Nay, nay, you need not bolt & locke so fast, Exit Eliz: Gage: Claren : & Constab. Shee is no starter; honorable Lords, Speake to the Queene she may haue some release. But if this tyme should alter, marke me well, Could this be answer'd, could it fellow Peeres? I thinke not so. Gods marry deere, but it shall not be, Lord Howard ioyne with me, weele to the King. Come come my Lords, why do you staye so long, The Queenes high fauor shall amend this wrong. My Lord, it is the pleasure of the Queene, The prisoner Princesse should haue all the vse Of the lieftenants garden, the Queenes lodgings, And all the liberty this place affords. You may goe aske her and you will my Lord, Moreouer tis her highnes furder pleasure, That her sworne seruants shal attend on her, Two gentlemen of her Ewry, two of her Pantry, Two of her Kitchin, and two of her wardrobe, Besydes this gentleman here master Gage. Letters my Lord, it is impossible. Charing crosse my Liege. Your Grace may purchase glory from aboue, And intyer loue from all your peoples hearts, To make attonement twixt the wofull Princesse, And our dread soueraigne, your most vertuous Queene. O my Lord, you speake not charitably. See my Lord, a warrant for the Princesse death Before she be conuicted, what iugling call you this? See, see for Gods sake. Whose plot was this? How was't reueald? He hath shewd his loue to the King & Queenes maiestyes, His seruice to his Country, and care of the Princesse. Winchester's dead, O God vppon euen at his death, He shewd his mallice to the sweete young Princesse, God pardon him, his soule must answere all, She's still preseru'd, and still her foes do fall, The Queene is much besotted on these Prelates, For ther's another rays'd more base then he, Poole that Arch, for truth and honestie. Let him goe, why, then ther's a fall of Prelates. This realme will neuer stand in perfect state, Till all their faction be cleare ruinate. How hard you that? The state begins to alter. Gods will be done; whose with the Queene, my Lord? VVee'le waight vpon their Honors. Exeunt omnes. The imperiall Crowne, I here present your Grace, With it my staffe of Office and my place. You are in your loue as free as in your care, You're come euen iust a day after the fayre.
speeches.Cha:: The Cardinall of Winchester : The Lord of Tame : the good Lord Shandoyse : and besides, Lo: Howard, Sir Henry Beningfeild, and diuers others.
speeches.Shand:: Tuching the Queene my Lord who now sitts hye, What thinks the realme of Phillip th'Emperours sonne, A marriage by the Councell treated of? I cry your Honors mercy. Resolue the Princesse we must speake with her. Tis from the Queene and wee will speake with her. Madam, our messuage and our duty from our Queene, Wee come to tender you, It is her pleasure, That you the 7. day of this moneth appeare at Westminster. Is your opinion so? So sayes the Queene. Madam, the Queene hath sent her letter for you. What answere you to Sir Peter Carew in the west, The westerne Rebels. My Lord, my Lord, let not the loue we beare the Prin cesse, incurre the Queenes displeasure, tis no dallying with mat ters of Estate, who dares gaine-say the Queene? My Lord, you must looke into our Commission, No fauors granted, she of force must land, Tis a decree which we can not with stand, So tell her master Gage, Exit Gage. The Sword of Iustice on my bended knee, I to your Grace present, heauen blesse your raigne.
speeches.Tame:: Pray god 't prooue well. Good morrow my good Lord of Sussex. The like to you my Lord: As you were speaking With all my hart Lord Howard. Goe tell her we must and will. It shall not neede, presse after her my Lord. Sorry we are sweet Lady, to behold you in this sad plight. Doctor Owine and Doctor Wendith, You are the Queenes Phisitions truly sworne, On your alegeance, as before her highnes you will answere it, Speake, may the Princesse be remoou'd with life. Madam, we take no pleasure to deliuer so strict a messuage. To morrow earlie then you must prepare. What answere you to Wiats late rebellion, Madam, tis thought that you did set them on. Rowme for the Lords there. Exeunt Counsell. Madam it raynes. A gentleman in fauor with the Queene. Alas Sir Harry these are honest contrey men, That much reioyce to see the Princesse well. And myne as great as yours. Bells. Madam this night your lodging's at my house, No prisoner are you Madame for this night. No, no prisoner, what I intend to do ile answere, Madame, wil't please you goe. Exit Eliz: Bening: & Tame. You much amaze me sir, els heauen forefend. And I with you would spend my deerest blood, To do that vertuous Lady any good. Sir Harry, now my charge I must resigne, The Ladye's wholy in your custody, Yet vse her kindly as she well deserues, And so I take my leaue, Madame adue. Exit Tame How now my masters what's here to do. And you do well: and yet me thinke 'twere fit, To spend some funerall teares vpon her hearce. VVho while she liu'd was deere vnto you all. Did you not loue her father when he liu'd, As deerly as you ere did loue any, And yet reioyced at his funerall: Likewise her brother 〈…〉 em'd him deere, Yet once departed, ioyfully you sung, Runne to make Bone-fiers, to proclaime your loue Vnto the newe, forgetting still the old: Now she is gone, how you mone for her, VVere it not fit a while to mone her hearse, And dutyfully there reioyce the tother; Had you the wisest and the louingst Prince, That euer swayd a Scepter in the world, This is the loue he shall haue after life: Let Princes while they liue haue loue or feare 'tis fit, For after death, ther's none continues it. I blame you not, nor do I you commend, For you will still the strongest side defend. Exit. This Garter with the order of the George, Two Ornaments vnto the Crowne of England, I here present.
speeches.Chamb:: Good morrow to the Lords of Tame and Shandoyse. Good morrow good Lord Howard.
speeches.Bening:: Concerning Wiatt and the Kentish rebels, Their ouer-throw is past: the rebell Dukes that sought By all meanes to proclaime queene Iane cheifly Northumberland For Gilfords sake, he for'st his brother Duke vnto that warre, But each one had his merite. Pardon my Lord I sawe you not till now. Such is your sister, A meere opposite to vs in our opinion, and besides Shees next Successiue, should your maiesty Dye yssules, which heauen defend. The state of our religion would decline. The bargmen were too desperat my Lord, In staying till the water was so lowe, For then you know, being vnderneath the bridge, The barges sterne did strike vppon the ground, And was in danger to haue dround vs all. But that will neuer be, this is my censure, If she be guilty in the least degree, May all her wronges suruiue and light on her: If other wayes that she be cleered, Thus both wayes I wish her downe, Or els her state to rayse. Come madam will you goe. what traytor knaues are gather'd here to make a tumult? If they persist, I charge you soldiers stop their mouthes. My lord my Lord, my charge is great. Traytors and knaues ring Bells, When the Queenes enemy passeth through the towne, Goe set he knaues by'th heales, make their pates ring noone, I charge thee Barwick. Exit Barwick. Come come away, this lingring will benight vs. How? no prisoner. Barwicke, is this the chayre of state. Take it downe, and pull of my boots. Well sayd Barwick, pull knaue. Well sayd, now comes. What saucy arrant knaue art thou, how? Villaine thou hast broken my crooper. Knaue, doest flout me? Exeunt. He beats him out. What to do Madam. I finde not that in my Commission. No Iaylor, but your gardian Madam. Madam I dare not, my Commission serues not. Good madam I entreate you loose that name Of Iaylor, twilbe a by-word to me and my posterity. Say I should reach you pen, inke and paper, Who ist dare beare a letter sent from you. Who euer dares, none shall. Baddy of me, what a bold knaue's this? What has she written here? He reads. Much suspected by me, nothing prou'd can be, Finis quoth Elizabeth the prisoner, Pray god it proue so, soft what book's this, Marry a God, whats here an English bible? Sanctum Maria pardon this prophanation of my hart, Water Barwick, water, Ile meddle with't no more. Your letter shalbe forth-comming Lady, I will pervse it ere it scape me now. Exit Beningfeild. Here haue you writ a long excuse it seemes, But no submission to the Queene your sister. I doe write and send, Ile crosse you still; She shall not speake to any man aliue, But ile ore-heare her, no letter nor no token Shall euer haue accesse vnto her hands, But first ile see it; So like a subiect to my soueraigns state, I will pursue her with my deadly hate. how knaue, with the Princesse? she parted euen now. Heer's for thy paynes, thou art an honest fellow: Goe take a Gard and apprehend them straight. Exit Clowne. Bring them before me, O this was well found out, Now will the Queene commend my diligent care, And prayse me for my seruice to her grace. Ha, traytors swarme so neere about my house, Tis time to looke into't: O well said Barwick, Wher's the prisoner. Lord blesse vs, knaue what hast thou there? Why knaue, this is a beast. VVhat art thou knaue? A kinne to mee, knaue ile haue thee whipt. Nay, but doest thou flout me still. He beats him. VVhat, droopes your honor? Exeunt omnes Phil: & Queene. Come come my Lord, this is but for a show, Our Queene I warrant wishes in her hart, Her sister Princesse were without her head. Long liue the Queene, long liue your Maiesty, I haue bid hard to be the first reporter, Of these glad tydings first; and all these here.
speeches.Howard:: Oh my Lord, The Lawe proceeded gainst their great offence, And 'tis not well, since they haue suffered Iudgment, That we should rayse their scandall being dead, Tis impious, not by true Iudgment bread. Prepare you Lords with our fayre Queene to ride, And his high princely state lett no man hide. Madam he would not. Which way lyes the Princesse. This wilbe glad tydings: come let's tell her grace. Stay your Imperiall hand, let not your seale imprint Deaths impresse in your sisters hart. Where is the Princesse. Madam she will, this night she hath appoynted, That she her selfe in person meanes to heare you, Protract no time, then come let's hast away. Exeunt.
speeches.Howa:: Your honors; The like to you my Lords.
speeches.Winch:: Good morrow Lords, attend the Queene into the pre sence. And reason fellow. Madam, here is a large recitall & vpbraydinge of your highnes Soueraignty, the Suffolke men that lifted you to the throne, and heere possest you, claime your promise you made them about re ligion. May't please your highnes note the Commons insolence They tye you to conditions, and set lymits to your liking. Away with him, it shalbe throughly scand, And you vppon the pillory, three dayes to stand. Exit Dodds. And well remembred, is't not probable, That she in Wiats expedicion, And other insurrection lately queald Was a confederate; if your highnes wil your owne estate preserue, You must foresee fore-danger, and cut off all such As would your safetie preiudice. Doe not you heare, with what a sawcye impudence, This Sentlo heere presumes. Twilbe a meanes to keepe the rest in awe, Making their soueraignes brow, to them a lawe. Young Courtney Earle of Devonshire, Seemes cheifly to affect her faction. Madam, we from the Queene are ioynd They sit, shee kneeles. in full commission. Madam, perhaps you censure hardly. That was enforst in this commission. Madam I would you would submit, vnto her highnes. Come Madam, answere breifly to these treasons. Then Madam you'le not submit. You are stubborne, come letts certifie the Queene. It is the pleasure of her maiestie, That you be straight committed to the Tower. Moreouer all your howshold seruants we haue dis charg'd, Except this gentleman your vsher & this gentlewoman Thus did the Queene commaund, And for your guard, a hundred Northern whitecotes, Are appoynted to conduct you thither, To night vnto your chamber, to morrow early prepare You for the Tower, your bardge stands ready, To conduct you thyther. shee kneeles. My Lord, you know it is in vaine, For the Queenes sentence is definitiue, And we must see't perform'd. Did you not marke what a pitious eie she cast To the Queens window as she past a long, Fayne she would haue stayd, but that I caus'd The bargmen to make hast and row away. Well she hath scapt that danger, Would she but conforme her selfe in her opinion, She only might rely vppon my loue, To winne her to the fauour of the Queene. Here comes the Constable of the tower, This is your charge. Madam the Queene out of her royall bounty, Hath freed you from the thraldome of the tower, And now this gentleman must be your gardyan. I thanke her: she hath ryd me of a Tyrant, Is he appoynted now to be my keeper? What is he Lordes? I know your busines, and your hast shall stay, As you were speaking my Lord Constable. Fellow what then: This warrant that concernes The Princesse death, shuffle amongst the rest, Hee'le nere peru'st. Stand ready purseuant, Exit Gresham. That when tis sign'd, Thou mayst be gone, and gallope with the winde. Oh chance accurst, how came he by this notice? Her life is garded by the hand of heauen, And we in vaine pursue it. Oh, I am sicke. VVhere yours and all good subiects els should lye, Neere at the hart, this confirmation I doe greatly dread, For now our true religion will decay, I do diuine who euer liues seauen yeare, Shall see no Religion here but heresye. No, no my Lords, this peace is naturall, This combination is without deceyt, But I will once more write to incence the Queene, The plot is laid, thus it shalbe perform'd: Sir Harry, you shall goe attach her seuant Vppon suspition, of some trechery, VVherin the Princesse shalbe accessary, If this do faile, my pollicy is downe, But I grow faynt, the feauer steales on me, Death like a vulture tyres vpon my hart, Ile leaue you two to prosecute this drift, My bones to earth I giue, to heauen my soule lift.
speeches.Quee:: By gods assistance and the power of heauen, We are instated in our brothers throane, And all those powers, that war'd against our right, By helpe of heauen and your freindly ayde, Disper'stand fled, heere may we sit secure, Our hearts is ioyfull Lords, our peace is pure. O master Dodds we are indebted to you for your loue, You stood vs in great stead even in our ebb Of fortune, when our hopes were neere declin'd, And when our state did beare the lowest saile, Which we haue reason to requit wee know; Read his peticion my good Lord Cardinall. Away with him, ile teach him know his place, To frowne when we frowne, smile on whome we grace. All those that seeke our sisters cause to fauour, Let them be lodged. Commit him to the Tower, Till time affordes vs and our Counsell breathing space. Whence is that Post? A Horne within. Our Secretary, vnseale them and returne Vs present answere of the contents, She speakes to the Lo: Constable. Whats the mayne busines. Prepare to meete him Lords with all our Pompe. Set forwad Lords, this sodaine newes is sweete, Two royall louers on the midde way meere. Exeunt omnes. Let her attend, we will find time to heare her. My Lord of VVinchester, my Lord of Sussex. Lord Howard, Tame, and Shandoyse, Take you Commission to examine her Of all supposed Crimes; so to our Nuptials. Where is the Princesse. Vsher her in by torch light. Our fauor shalbe farre boue her desert, And she that hath been banisht from the light, Shall once againe behold our cheerfull sight. You my Lord shall step behind the arras, And heare our conference, weele shew her Grace, For there shines too much mercy in your face. Wherefore do you cry? To see your selfe so low, or vs so hye. Sister, I rather thinke they're teares of spleene. I, that's your greefe. You'le not submit but end as you begin. You are not guilty then? I am not of your mind. How meane you that. You haue been wrong imprison'd then. VVhat ere we thinke aryse and kisse our hand, Say God hath rais'd you frends. Promise, why? Sister this night your selfe shall feast with me, To morrow for the country you are free, Lights for the Princesse conduct her to her chamber. Exit Eliz: VVhy should two harts be for'st to seperate, I know your busines but beleeue me sweete, My soule diuines we neuer more shall meete.
speeches.Dodds:: I doe beseech your maiestie peruse this poore peticion. True gratious Soueraigne; But that we doe vpbraid your maiestie, Or make recitall of our deedes forepast, Other then conscience, honesty and zeale, By loue, by faith, and by our dutie bound, To you the next and true successiue heyre, If you contrary this; I needs must say, Your skillesse tongue doeth make our well tun'd wordes, Iarr in the Princes eares, and of our text, You make a wronge construction: Gratious Queene, Your humble subiects prostrate in my mouth, A generall suit when we first flockt to you, And made first head with you at Framagham, Twas thus concluded that we your liegemen: Should still enioy our consciences, and vse that faith Which in king Edwards daies was held Canonicall.
Oh gratious soueraigne, let my Lord the Duke haue the Perusing of it, or any other that is neere your grace, He will be to our suit an opposite.
speeches.Queen:: They shall know, To whome their faithfull duties they doe owe, Since they the lymbes, the head would seeke to sway, Before they gouerne, they shall learne t'obays See it seuerely ordred Winchester. My Lord of Tame and Shandoyse, You two shall haue a firme Commission seal'd, To fetch our sister young Elizabeth From Ashbridge where shee lyes, and with a band Of armed souldiers to conduct her vp to London, Where we will heare her.
speeches.Benif:: Has not your sister (gratious Queene) a hand In these peticions; well your highnes knowes She is a fauorite of these heritiques.
Which heauen defend. Long liue the King and Queene. Florish.
speeches.Sentlo:: Gratious Queene, she only craues but to behold your face, That she might cleare her selfe of all supposed treasons, Still protesting, she is as true a subiect to your grace, As liues this day.
speeches.Const:: My Soueraigne, It is from Southampton. That Phillip Prince of Spaine, Sonne to the Emperour, is safely ariu'd, And landed at Southampton. The Lord of Tame and Shandoyse are return'd. Madam, the Queene must here you sing another song, Before you parte with vs. And I receiue my prisoner, come will you goe? Here's no chayre for prisoners, Come will you see your chamber. Tush tush the Queene is young likely to beare, Of her owne body a more royall heyre. Twas my appoyntment, and it shalbe so. Now sir, what haue you got by your Exeunt omnes, praeter Consta. and Gage. complayning, you common find-fault; what, is your Mistresse stomacke so queasie? our honest souldiers must not touch her meat, then let her fast, I know her stomacke will come downe at last. Presume to touch a dish Ile lodge thee there, Where thou shalt see no sunne for one hole yeare. Come talke not to me for I am resolu'd, Nor lodging, garden, nor lieftenants walkes Shall here be granted, shee's a prisoner. How, shall they knaue? What meanes her grace by that? The next wilbe her freedom, oh this madds me. This way my Lord. This base groome flowts me, oh this frets my hart, These knaues will let vpon their priuiledge, But yet ile vex her, I haue found the meanes, Ile haue my cookes to dresse my meate with hers, And euerie officer my men shall match, Oh that I could but draine her harts deare blood, Oh it would feede me, do my soule much good. How now, what meanes the fellow. Sir 'twas my pleasure and I did command it. No Sir, why say 'tis I. You will not. Stay him stay him, oh haue I caught you Sir, Where haue you been. A crafty knaue my Lords, serch him for letters. Come tell me what letters thou carryedst her, Ile giue thee figgs and suger plummes. Now tell me what letters thou deliuerest. Yes marry will I, take him away, Let him be soundly whipt I charge you sirra. My Lord she's factious, rather could I wish She were marryed to some priuat gentleman, And with her dower conuaid out of the land, Then here to stay and be a mutiner, So may your highnes state be more secure. For whilst she liues warres, and commotions, Foule insurrections wilbe set abroch, I thinke 'twere not amisse to take her head: This land would be in quiet, were she dead. When as the King shall come to seale these writes. Sir, Harry do you heare the whispring in the Court, They say the Queene is craysy very ill. Tis common through the house. This Cap of mayntenance, I present my state of Office, and my vtmost seruice. Pardon me gratious Madame 'twas not spleene, But that alegance that I ow'd my Queene, Madame I seru'd her truly at that day, And I as truly will your Grace obay,
Good morrow Mistresse, came you from the Princesse? How fares her Grace. How now what's the matter. Heauen guard the Princesse grant that all be well, This Drumme I feare, will prooue her passing-bell. O my honor'd Lords, (May I with reuerence presume to aske) What meanes these armes, why doe you thus begirt, A poore weake Lady, neere at poynt of death. You are deny'd that grace: Her Maiestie will not admitt you conference, Sir William Sentlo vrging that motion, VVas first committed, since sent to the Tower, Madam, in breife your foes are the Queenes freindes, Your freinds her foes, Six of the Counsell are this day appoynted, To examine you of certaine articles, My grieued Mistresse humbly thus intreats, For to remooue backe to the Common stayres, And not to land where Traytors put to shore, Some difference she intreats your Honors make Twixt Christall Fountaines, and fowle muddy Springs, Twixt those that are condemned by the law, And those whome Treasons staine did neuer blemish: Thus she attends your answere, and sits still Whilst her wet eyes, full many a teare did spill. My honor'd Lord, why should you take delight To torture a poore Lady innocent? The Queene I know when she shall heare of this, Will greatly discommend your crueltie. You seru'd her father, and he lou'd you well, You seru'd her brother, and he held you deare, And can you hate the sister he best lou'd? You serue her sister, she esteemes you hye, And you may liue to serue her ere you dye: And therefore good my Lord, let this preuaile, Only the casements of her window ope, Whereby she may receiue fresh gladsome ayre.
speeches.Wom:: Master Gage, I did. Ile certifie so much. Exit Woman Her grace intreates you but to stay till morne? And then your message shalbe heard at full. Ile certifie so much. Wher's mistres Clarential to horse to horse, The Princesse is sent for to the Court Shee's gone already, come let's after.
speeches.Woman:: O wondrous crazey gentle master Gage, Her sleepes are all vnquiet, and her head Bears and growes giddy with continuall griefe. My Lords, know there is no admittance to her presence, VVithout the leaue, first granted from her selfe.
speeches.Gage:: God grant her comfort, and release her paine, So good a Ladie few on earth remaine. My Lords, as you are honorably borne, As you did loue her father, or her brother, As you do owe alegeance to the Queene, In pitty of her weaknes, and lowe state, With best of fauor, her commisserate. He that first gaue you life, protect that life, From those that wish your death. Madam, that the Queene & VVinchester best knowes. Madam, we your poore humble seruants, Made bold to presse into your graces presence, To know how your cause goes. That shall be my charge my Lord. Exit Gage. Madam, you haue stept too short into the water. My Lords the Princesse humbly entreats, That her owne seruants may beare vp her dyet, A company of base vntutord slaues, Whose hands did neuer serue a Princesse boord, Do take that priuiledge. Stay good my Lords for instance, see they come, If this be seemly, let your honors Iudge. Vntutor'd slaue, Ile ease thee of this burden, Her highnes scornes to touch the dishe Her seruants brings not vp. I would to god you would, in any place Exit Const: & souldiers. Where I might liue from thought of her disgrace, O thou all-seeing heauens, with pitious eies, Looke on th'oppresions of their cruelty! Let not thy truth, by falshood be opprest, But let her vertues shyne and giue her rest, Confound the sleights, and practise of those men, Whose pride do kicke against thy seat of heauen. Oh draw the courtaines from their filthy sinne, And make them loath the hell which they liue in. Prosper the Princesse, and her life defend, A glorious comfort to her troubles send. If euer thou hadst pittie, heare my prayer, And giue releasement to a Princes care. Exit Gage. The Princesse thus entreats you honor'd Lord, She may but walke in the Lieftenants garden, Or els repose her selfe in the Queens lodgings: My honor'd Lord, grant this as you did loue The famous Henry her deceased father. My Lord, they shall. If the Queene please, they shall. A noble and right reuerent Counsellor, Promist to begge it of her Maiestie: And if she say the word, my Lord she shall. Vppon my life it stands not. The townes-men of the country gathered here, To greete your Grace, hearing you past this way. The townes-men of this village, Hearing your highnes passe this way, Salutes your comming with this peale of Bells. They deepely coniur'd me out of their loues, To know how your case goes, which these poore people second. Thus did she bid me say tanquam Ouis, Farewell I must away. Exit Gage Out liue this night, I pray Madam why. O Madam, you were borne to better fortunes, That God that made you, will protect you still From all your enemies that wish you ill. O my honor'd Lord, As euer you were noble in your thoughts, Speake, shall my Lady out liue this night, or no? For if we should imagine any plott, Pretending to the hurt of our deere mistres, I and my fellowes though farre vnable are To stand against your power, will dy together. Madame, impose the letter to my trust, Were I to beare it through a feild of pikes, And in my way ten thousand arm'd men ambusht, Ide make my passage through the mid'st of them, And perforce beare it to the Queene your sister. Madame I fly, To giue this leter to her maiesty: Hoping when I returne, To giue you comfort that now sadly mourne. Exeunt omnes preter Ben: And a pursuiuant ready to post away with it, To see it doone with speede, What flynty brest could brooke to see her bleed? Good madam, blot such thoughts out of your minde, The Lords I knowe, are still about your sute, And make no doubt, but they will so preuaile Both with the King and Queene, that you shall see Their haynos anger wilbe turnd to loue. Madam Clarentia, is my Lady stirring? Heauen sheild my Mistres, and make her frends increase, Conuert her foes, estate her in true peace. Oh most vnhappy dreame, my feare is now As great as yours, before it was but small, Come let's goe comfort her, that ioyes vs all. Madame I see from farre a horse-man comming, This way he bends his speed he comes so fast, That he is couered in a cloud of dust, And now I haue lost his sight, he appear's againe, Making his way ouer Hill, Hedge, Ditch and Plaine: One after him, they two striue As on the race they had wagerd both their liues, Another after him. Strange and miraculous, the first being at the gate, His horse hath broke his necke, and cast his rider. Long liue the Queene, long liue your maiesty, I Captaine of your highnes Pentioners.
O Lord the house is beset, shouldiers are as hot as fier, Are reddy to enter euerie hole about the howse, For as I was a'th toppe of the stacke, the sound of the Drumme, Hott mee such a box a'th Eare, that I came tumbling downe, The stacke with a thousand byllets a'th top on me, looke about, And helpe for gods sake.
Wher's the Princesse. We found the Princesse, sicke and in great danger; Yet did we vrge our strickt Commission, She much intreated that she might be spar'd, Vntill her health and strength might be restor'd.
speeches.Eliz:: We are not pleas'd with your intrusions Lords. Is your hast such, of your affayres so vrgent, That sudenly, and at this tyme of night, You presse on one, and will not stay till morne? And I my Lords not glad, My hart, oh how it beats. My Inocence yet makes my hart as light, As my front's heauie: all that heauen sends is welcome Gentlemen diuide these few crownes amongst you, I am now a prisoner; and shall want nothing, I haue some friends about her maiesty, That are prouiding for mee all things; all things; I, euen my graue; and being possest of that, I shall need nothing: weepe not I pray, Rather you should reioyce: If I miscarry in this enterprise, and aske you why, A Virgine and a Martyr both I dy. VVhats my of offence? who be my accusers. VVhat saies the Queene vnto my late petition. They shalbe welcome; my god in whome I trust, VVill helpe, deliuer, saue, defend the iust. My duty with my fortunes do agree, And to the Queene in you I bend my knee. Knowe you your owne guilt my good Lord Chancelor, That you accuse your selfe, I thinke not so, I am of this mynd, no man is my foe. Submit my Lord of Winchester, tis fit That none but base offenders should submit, No no my Lord, I easily spy your drifte, Hauing nothing whereon you can accuse me, Do seeke to haue my selfe, my selfe betray, So by my selfe my owne blood should be spilt, Confesse submission I confesse a guilt. My reuerent Lord I know it. Oh my good Lord he could not. My god be prays'd, this is newes but of a minute old. Aske the vnborne Infant, see what that will answere, For that and I, are both alike in guilt, Let not by rigor Innocent blood be spilt. Treason Lords, if it be treason to be the daughter To th'Eight Henry ; Sister to Edward, and the next of blood vnto My gratious soueraigne now the Queene I am a traytor: if not, I Spit at treason. In Henryes raigne this Law could not haue stood, O god that we should suffer for our blood. My god doth know, I can no note but truth, That with heauens King, One day in quiers of Angels I shall singe. My life I will, but not as guilty, My Lords, let pale offendors pardon craue, If we offend, Lawes rigor let vs haue. Thou power eternall, Inocents iust guide, That sways the Scepter of all Monarchyes, Protect the guiltlesse from these rauening Iawes, That hidious death presentes, by Tyrants Lawes, And as my hart is knowne to thee most pure, Grant mee release, or patience to endure. Well, well, I thanke my god, well, How can a cause go ill with Innocents, They that to whome wronges in this world are done, Shalbe rewarded in the world to come. The Tower, for what? Oh god my hart: A prisoner in the Tower, Speake to the Queene my Lords, that some other place May lodge her sister, that's too vild, too base. Then to our chamber comfortlesse and sad, To morrow to the tower that fatall place, Where I shall neuer behold the sunnes bright face. No matter where I tread, Would where I set my foote, there lay my head, Land Traytor like; my foot's wet in the flood, So shall my hart ere long be drencht in blood. No let it a lone: See gentle men, The pittious heauens weepes teares into my bosome, On this cold stone I sit, raine in my face, But better heere, than in a worser place VVhere this bad man will lead me. Clarentia, reach my booke, now leade me where you please From sight of day; or in a dungeon; I shall see to pray. Welcome sweet boy, what hast thou brought me there. God a mercy boy, heeres to requite thy loue. They keepe euen infants from vs, they do well, My sight they haue too long bard, and now my smell, This tower hath made me fall to huswiffry, I spend my labors to releeue the poore, Goe Gage distribute these to those that neede. Yt seemes so by his charge, but tell me Gage, Is yet the scaffold standing on tower hill, Whereon young Gilford and the Lady Iane did suffer death. Lord Howard what is he. With all my hart, fare-well, far-well, I am freed from Lymbo to be sent to hell. Exeunt omnes. What are these? Giue them this Gold, and thanke them for their loues. Alas poore men, helpe them thou God aboue, Thus men are forst to suffer for my loue, What sayd my seruants, those that stood aloofe? Say to them tanquam Ouis. What fearefull terror doth assayle my hart? Good Gage come hether and resolue me true In thy opinion; shall I out liue this night, I pre thee speake. Then to be plaine this night I looke to die. My hart is fearefull. To write a letter to the Queene my sister. Good Iaylor vrge not thy Commission. Then reach me pen and inke. Thus you haue driuen me of from tyme to tyme, Still vrging me with your Commission. Good Iaylor be not so seuere. As often as you name your Commission, So often will I call you Iaylor. I do not keepe a seruant so dishonest, That would deny me that. Gage leaue me to my selfe, Thou euer liuing power, that giuest all harts, Giue to my pen, a true perswasiue stile, That it may moue my impatient sisters eares, And vrge her to compassionate my woe. Shee writes. My hart is heauye and my hart doth close, I am weary of writing, sleepy on the sodaine, Clarentia, leaue me, and command some musick In the with-drawing chamber. shee sleepes. O God, how pleasant was this sleepe to me? Clarentia, saw'st thou nothing? Nor heard'st thou nothing? Should they submit that neuer wrought offence, The Lawe will alwayes quit wrong'd Innocence: Gage, take my letter, to the Lords commend my humble duty. I wonder Gage that we haue stayd so long, So neere the Court, and yet haue heard no newes From our displeased sister, this more affrites me Then my former troubles, I feare this Hampton court Wilbe my graue. Welcome my good Lo: Howard what sayes the Queene, Will she admit my sight? That God that rais'd you, staye you, and protect You from your foes, and cleere me from suspect. Neither dread Queene, mine is a womanish teare, In part compeld by ioy, and part by feare: Ioy of your sight, these brinish teares haue bread, For feare of my Queenes frowne, to strike me dead. You were my sister, now you are my Queene. My life madam I will, but not as guilty, Should I confesse Fault done by her, that neuer did transgresse. Iioy to haue a sister Queene so royall, I would it as much pleas'd your maiesty, That you enioy a sister that's so true: If I were guilty of the least offence, Madame, 'twould taint the blood euen in your face, The treasons of the father being noble, Vnnobles all your children, let your grace Exact all torture and imprisonment, VVhat ere my greatest enemies can deuise, And they all haue done their worst, yet I VVill your true subiect and true sister dye. Madame to death I will, but not to sinne. I thinke I am not. I would your highnes were. To thinke as I thinke that my soule is cleere. Ile not say so. Then God hath kept his promise. To rayse them frends that on his word relie. O God, my last nights dreame I greatly feare, It doth presage my death, good master Gage Looke to the path-way that doth come from the court, I looke each minute for deaths messenger. Would he were here now, so my soule were pure, That I with patience might the stroke endure. O God, what meanes this hast? Pray for my soule, my life cannot long last. This same is but as prologue to my death, My heart is guiltlesse though they take my breath. God saue the Queene, so all good subiects say: I am her subiect, and for her still pray. This newes is sweete, my hart was sore affraid: Rise thou first Barron that we euer made. Thankes good Sir Iohn, we will deserue your loue. Lord Howard thankes you euer were our frend, I see your loue continues to the end, But cheefly, thanks to you my Lord of Hunsdon. The very same; His tongue was first proclaymer of our name: And trusly Gage in token of our Grace, We giue to you a captaine Pentioners place. We will descend & meete them. We thanke you all. Whil'st we this Crowne so long your place enioy. Keepe it my Lord, and with it be you hye admirall. Your loue we knowe. We do as freely pardon as you truly serue, Onely your staffe of Office weele displace, In stead of that weele owe you greater Grace, What's he, my Iaylor? Be not asham'd man, looke me in the face, VVho haue you now to patronize your strictnes on? For your kindnes this I will bestowe, When we haue one we would haue hardly vs'd And cruelly delt with, you shall be the man, This is a day for peace, not for vengeance fit, All your good deeds wee'le quit, all wronges remit. Where we left off, proceede. This Sword is ours, this staffe is yours againe. Possesse them still my Lord, what Offices beare you? Some we intend to rayse, none to displace; Lord Hunsdon, we will one day finde a staffe To poyse your hand: you are our Cosen, And deserue to be employd neerer our person: But now to you from whome we take this staffe, Since Cardinall Poole is now decea'st and dead, To shew all mallice from our breast is worne, Before you let that Purse and Mace be borne, And now to London Lords lead on the way, Praysing that King, that all Kings els obay. VVe thanke you all: but first this booke I kisse. Thou art the way to honor; thou to blisse, An English Bible, thankes my good Lord Maior, You of our bodie and our soule haue care, This is the Iewell that we still loue best, This was our solace when we were distrest, This booke that hath so long conceald it selfe, So long shut vp, so long hid; now Lords see, VVe here vnclaspe, for euer it is free: VVho lookes for ioy, let him this booke adore, This is true foode for rich men and for poore, VVho drinkes of this, is certaine nere to perish, This will the soule with heauenly vertue cherish, Lay hand vppon this Anchor euery soule, Your names shalbe in an eternall scrowle; VVho builds on this, dwel's in a happy state, This is the fountaine cleere imaculate, That happy yssue that shall vs succeed, And in our populous Kingdome this booke read: For them as for our owne selues we humbly pray, They may liue long and blest; so lead the way.
speeches.Eliza:: At Westminster ? my Lords no soule more glad then I, To doe my duty to her Maiestie, But I am sorry at the hart, my hart, oh good Doctor rayse me: Oh my hart, I hope my Lords, considering my excremity and Weaknes, you will dispence a little with your hast. Nor I my Lords to heare a messuage deliuered with such strictnes; well must I goe. Why then it must be so. Tis many a more 〈◊〉 my feeble leggs, Felt this my bodies waight: O I shall faynt, And if I tast the rawnes of the ayre, I am but dead, indeed I am but dead. Tis late, conduct these Lordes vnto their chambers, And cheere them well for they haue iorneyd hard, whilst we prepare vs for our morrowes Iorney. The Queene is 〈◊〉 , and we will striue with death To tender her our life, We are her subiect, and obay her hest, Good night, we wish you what wee want, Good rest. Exeunt omnes. Who is't will say so? men may much suspect, But yet my Lord, none can my life detect, I a confederate with those kentish rebells? Yf I ere saw or sent to them, let the Queene take my head, Hath not proud Wyat suffered for his offence, And in the purging both of soule and body for heauen, Did Wyat then accuse Elizabeth? Then on this stone, this cold stone I will sit, I needes must say you hardly me intreat, VVhen for a chayre, this hard stone is my seate. Hath he not thinke you a stretch conscience, And if my secret murder should be put into his hands, Hath he not hart thinke you to execute.
Not without danger Lords, yet without death, Her feauer is not mortall; yet you see into what danger, It hath brought the Princesse.
speeches.D: Wend:: My Iudgment is, not deadly, but yet dangerous, No sooner shall she come to take the ayre, But she will faint, and if not well prepar'd and attended, Her life is in much danger.
speeches.Que:: Thus in the face of heaue ̄ , & broad eie of all the multitude, We giue a welcome to the Spanish Prince, Those plausiue shouts which giue you entertaine, Ecchoes as much to the almighties cares, And there they sownd with pleasure, and excels The claymorous trumpetts, and loud ringing bells.
Thrise excellent and euer gracious Princesse, Doubly famous for vertue and for beautie, We embrace your large stretcht Honors with the armes of loue, Our Royall marriage, treated first in Heauen To be solemniz'd here, both by Gods voice, And by our loues consent, we thus embrace: Now Spaine and England two populous Kingdomes, That haue a long time been oppos'd In Hostile-emulation, shalbe at one: This shalbe Spanish England, ours English Spaine. Then here before the 〈◊〉 of the Land, We doe embrace and make a publique contract. Our soules are ioyfull, then bright Heauens smile, Whil'st we proclaime our new vnited Stile. It likes vs well, but royall Queene we want One Ladie at this hye solemnitie: We haue a Sister cal'd Elixaebeth, Whose vertues and endowments of the mind Hath fil'd the eares of Spaine. But royall Queene, yet for her vertues sake, Deeme her offences, if she haue offended, VVith all the lenitie a Sister can. VVhat Festiuall more Royall hath been seene, Than twixt Spaines Prince, and Englands Royall Queene.
Harke the redoubling ecchoes of the people, Florish. How it proclaymes their loues; and welcome to this Vnion. How fares our Sister? Is she come alonge? Call the Princesse. Exeunt for the Princesse, Phillip behind the arras. All forbeare this place, except our sister now? Exeunt omnes. Wee know you can speake well: will you submit?
Read Sussex. Phillip and Mary, by the grace of God, King and Queene of England, Spayne, France and Ireland, King and Queene of Naples, Scifcillia, Leon and Aragon, Arch. When please your Highnesse to solemnize this your Nup tials?
speeches.Qu:: The 25. day of this month Iuly.
Great are the causes, now too long to say, Why she my Soueraigne should be kept away.
Two of your Highnesse Doctors we then cal'd, And charg'd them as they would answere it, To tell the truth, if that our iourneys toyle Might be no preiudice vnto her life; Or if we might with safetie bring her thence: They answered, that we might; we did so, Here she is to doe her dutie to your Maiestie.
speeches.Eli:: Is not my gentleman vsher yet return'd.
O God, my feare hath been good phisick, But the Queens displeasure, that hath cur'd my bodies Imperfectio ̄ , Hath made me hart sick, braine sick, and sick euen to death. What are you? VVe thanke you, and am more indebted for your loues Than we haue power: or vertue to requite, Alas I am all the Queenes, yet nothing of my selfe, But God and Inocence, be you my Patrons and defend my cause VVhy weepe you gentlemen? Whither my Lord, vnto a grate of Iron, Where greife and care my poore hart shall enuirone, I am not well. Yt shall not need the poore are louing, but the rich despise, And though you curbe their tongue, spare them their eyes, Your loue my smart alwaies not but prolonges, Pray for me in your harts, not with your tongues, See see my Lord, looke I haue stild them all, Not one amongst them, but debates my fall. Madame, he was my foe, and not your freind That hath possest you so, I am as true a Subiect to your Grace, as any liues this day, Did you but see, My heart it bends, farre lower than my knee.
speeches.1. Ser:: Your howshold Officers and humble seruants, VVho now your house faire Princesse, is desolu'd And quite broke vp, come to attend your grace.
speeches.Cookes:: Not for our selues, men are not made to weepe At there owne fortunes, our eies are made of fire, And to extract water from fire is hard, Nothing but such a Princesse griefe as yours, So good a Ladie & so beautifull, so absolute a mistris, And perfect as you haue deliuered been, Haue power to doo't, your sorrow makes vs sad.
speeches.Sussex:: By your Fauour good my Lord ere you proceed, Madam, although this place doth tye you to this reuerence, It becomes not you being a Princesse to deiect your knee, A chaire there. A chayre for the Princesse.
speeches.1:: Come my masters you know your chardge, tis now about Alcauin, here we must watche till morning, And then carry the Princesse to the tower. Not I, Ile not meddle with the state, I hope this a man may say without offence, Prethee drincke to me. Masse I say this: That the Lady Elizabeth is both a lady, And Elizabeth, and if I should say she were a vertuous Princesse, Were there any harme in that? Well sirs I haue two sisters, and the one loues the other, And would not send her to prison for a million, is there any harme In this? ile keepe my selfe within compas I warrant you, For I doe not talke of the Queene, I talke of my sisters, Ile keepe my selfe within my compas I warrant you. Why Sir, I hope a man may be bold with his owne, I learn'd that of the Queene, Ile keepe my selfe within compasse Ile warrant you. It may be she doth not knowe her selfe, It may be the Queene knowes not the cause, It may be my Lord of Winchester does not know, It may be so, nothing's vnpossible to god, It may be ther's knauery in Munckery, Ther's nothing vnpossible, is there any harme in that? Why, in saying nothing's vnpossible to God, Ile stand to it; for saying a truth's a truth, ile proue it; For saying there may be knauerie in Monckery, Ile iustifie it, I do not say there is, but may be, I know what I know, You know what you know, he knowes what he knowes, Marry we know not what euery man knowes. I think so too, is there any harme in all this? Come then let's goe, would all were well, Is there any harme in all this? but alas wishes and teares Haue both one property, they shew their loue that Exeunt omnes. want the remedy.
speeches.2:: How shall we spend the time till morning. I but my frnd, do not talke of state matters. No by my troth, ther's no harme in that, But beware of talking of the Princesse, Let's meddle with our kindred there, we may be bold. I but Sir, why is the Princesse committed? Shoomaker, you goe a little beyond your last. No harme ith world.
speeches.3:: Mase weele drinck and talke of our frendes. I but Sir, that word sister goes hardly downe. My masters, we haue talkt so long that I thinke tis day. And I thinke by this time the Princesse is ready To take her barge.
Withall my harry faith, this a man might Lawfully speake, but now, faith what wast about to say.
So so, let me alone, let me alone to coope her, Ile vse her so, the Queene shall muth commend My diligent care.
VVhere haue you left the Princesse?
VVhere she is safe ynough I warrant you, I haue not granted her the priuiledge Of any walke, or garden, or to ope Her windowes, casements to receiue the ayre. My Lord, I hope I know mine office well, And better than your selfe within this place, Then teach not me my dutie, she shalbe vsd so still, The Queene commands, and Ile obay her will, I, if she say the word, it shalbe so: My lord of Winchester speakes the contrarie, So doe the Clergie, they are honest men. O you preach well to deafe men, no, not I, So letters may fly in, Ile none of that, She is my prisoner, and if I durst, But that my warrant is not yet so strickt, Ide lay her in a dungeon where her eyes, Should not haue light to read her prayer booke, So would I danger both her soule and body, Cause she an alyen is to vs catholiques, Her bed should be all snakes, her rest dispayre, Torture should make her curse, her faythles prayer. Well, Ile haue this amended er't be long, And venge my selfe on her for all their wrong.
My lord, my lord, you deale without respect, And worse than your Commission can mainetaine. What's the matter say: how fayres the Queene?
speeches.Gage,: Wilt please your honor, let my Lady Exeunt omnes preter Constable & Gage. Walke in the leiftenants garden, Or may but see the lodgings of the Queene, Or ope the casements to receiue fresh ayre, Shall shee my Lord: shall shee this freedom vse, Shee shall: for you can neither will nor chuse, Or shall shee haue some seruants of her owne, To attend on her: I pray let it be so, And let your looke no more poore prisoners daunt, I pray deny not what you needes must grant. Exit Gage.
speeches.Cooke:: Audacious slaue presuming in my place. The prowdest he that keepes within the tower, Shall haue no eie into my priuate office. Be it your selfe or any other here, Ile make him sup the hottest broth I haue. Zoundes I will, I haue been true to her, and will be still. Exit Cooke. What storme comes next: this hath disperst vs quite And shattered vs to nothing; though we be deny'd the presence Of our mistres, yet we will walke a loofe, and none controwle vs. Now gentle master vsher, what sayes my Lady. My selfe haue been a scholler, and I vnderstand What tanquam Ouis meanes. We sent to know how her Grace did fare, Shee, tanquam Ouis said, euen like a sheep, That's to the slaughter led.
I haue got another Nosegay for my young Lady, My Lord said I should be soundly whipt If I were seene to bring her any more, But yet Ile venture once againe, shee's so good, Oh heer's her chamber, Ile call and see if shee be stirring, Where are you Lady?
speeches.Boy:: Madam, I haue brought you another nose gay, But you must not let it be seene, for if it be, I shall be soundly whipt, indeedla, indeed I shall. To carry my younge Lady some more flowers, Will you indeed, well ile take your word, For you looke like an honest man. Faith gaffer I know no letters but great A, B and C: I am not come to K yet, Now gaffer will you giue me my suger plummes.
speeches.How:: Alas my Lord a child, pray let him goe. A gentleman, tho of a sterne aspect, Yet milde enough I hope your Grace will finde. Defend it heauen, and Gods almightie hand, Betwixt your Grace, and such intendments stand. Pardon him my Lord. It were a deed worthy of memory. The Chancelor and that iniuryous Lord, Can well expound the meaning. The Chancelors and my Lord Constables. By this gentleman Master Gresham the Kings Agent here. She waights your pleasure at the common stayers. Gentlemen vshers, & gentlemen Pentioners, lights For the Princesse, attendance gentlemen. Tis a sad Court my Lord. Whether in sorrow for the Kings departure, Or els for greife at Winchesters decease, Or els that Cardinall Poole is sodaynely dead, I cannot tell, but shee's exceeding sick. Nay more my Lord, I came now from the presence, I heard the Doctors whisper it in seecret, There is no way but one. The Duke of Norfolke, the Earle of Oxford, The Earle of Arundell, and diuers others, They are with-drawne into the inward chamber, There to take counsell, and intreat your presence. Though third in order, yet the first in loue, I tender my allegeance to your Grace, Liue long faire Queene, thrise happy be your raygne, He that instates you, your high state mayntayne. Meaning this Gentleman? Madame the Counsell are here hard at hand. Th'mperiall Scepter here I offer vp.
speeches.Pant:: Here will she crosse the riuer, stand in her eie, That she may take some notice of our neglected dutyes,
Come this way they say, the sweete Princesse comes, Let vs presente her with such tokens of good will, As we haue. Tanqus Ovrus pray whats tanqus Ovrus neighbor. Tanqus Ovrus, that I should liue to see, tanqus Ovris.
They say shee's such a vertuous Princesse, that sheele except of a cupp of cold water, and I haue euen a nosegay for her Grace, here she comes. If the preist were here hee'd smell it out straight. I shall nere loue tanquam Ovris againe for this tricke.
speeches.Omnes:: The Lord preserue thy sweete Grace. Now the Lord blesse thy sweete Grace. Long liue, long raigne our Soueraigne.
Harke harke my Lord, what Bells are these? God preserue your Grace.
speeches.Bar:: I sir, this is it. Come on Sir. A ha Sir. The Clowne pulls the Chayre from vnder him.
speeches.Clowne:: O monstrous, what a sawey companion's this? To pull of his boots in the chayre of state, Ile fit you a penyworth for it. O Sir Harry, you looke well to your office, Yonders one in the garden with the Princesse. I sir thats all one, but she no sooner came into the Garden, but he leapt ore the wall, and there They are together busie in talke Sir. Here he is in a string my Lord. This is he I told you was busie in talke with the Princesse; What a did there, you must get out of him by examination. So may your worship be for any thing that I know. Yf you worship does not remember me, I hope your worships crooper doth: But if you haue any thing to say to this honest fellow, VVho for his gray head and reuerent beard is so like, He may be a kinne to you. Then your worship will cry quittance with my Posteriors for misvsing of yours.
speeches.Clo:: Gods pitty I thinke you are downe, cry you mercy. Not so sawcy an arrant knaue as your worship takes me to be. I am sorry 'tis no worse for your worship. Whether goe you so fast mistris Clarentia. A milking, that's a poore office for a Madame. Troth you say true, euery one to his fortune, As men goe to hanging, the tyme hath been, When I would ha scorn'd to carry coles, but now the case is alter'd, Euery man as far as his tallent will stretch. Faith making Bone-fires for ioy of the newe Queene, Come sir your penny, and you be a true subiect, You'le battle with vs your faggot, we'lbe merry yfayth. By my fayth my masters, he speakes wisely, Come weele to the end of the lane, and there weele Make a bonfire and be merry, Fayth agreed ile spend my halfepenny towards Another faggot, rather then the newe Queene shall VVant a Bone-fire. Exeunt manet Tame.
speeches.Spa:: The wall, the wall. Seignior Caualero Danglatero, I must haue the wall. O base Caualero, my sword and ponyard well Try'd in Tolledo, shall giue thee the Imbrocado. Holo holo, thou hast giuen me The Canuissado. Seignior Caualero looke behint thee, A blade of Tolledo is drawne against thee. Oh vostro mandado grand Emperato.
speeches.Eng:: Sblood Spaniard you get no wall here, vnlesse you would Haue your head and the wall knockt together. I do protest, hadst not thou enforst it, I had not regarded it, but since you will needs Haue the wall, Ile take the paynes to thrust You into the kennell. Come Sir will you any more.
speeches.Eng: Marry, and welcome Sir, come on. They fight, he hurts the Spaniard.
speeches.Phill:: Hand that Ignoble groome, Had we not beheld thy cowardice, We should haue sworne, Such basenes had not followed vs. Are you respectles of our honor Lords, That you would haue vs bosome cowardice, I do protest the great turkes Empire, Shall not redeeme thee from a fellons death, What place is this my Lords? Then by this crosse, where thou hast done this murder, Thou shalt be hang'd, so Lords away with him. Exit Spaniard. Nor will we Lords embrace his heedles counsell, I doe protest as I am King of Spaine, My vtmost power ile stretch to make them frends, Come Lords let's in, my loue and wit ile try To end this Iarre; the Queene shall not deny. Exeunt omnes. Lord Chancelor, your dealing is not fayre, See Lords, what writs affords it selfe To the impresse of our scale. Lord Chancelor, out of our prerogatiue We will make bold to enterlyne your warrant. In stead of charging of the Sheriffes with her, We here discharge her keeper Beningfeild: And where we should haue brought her to the blocke, We now will haue her brought to Hampton court, There to attend the pleasure of the Queene, The Pursuiuant that should haue posted downe With tydings of her death, Beare her the messuage of her repriued life, You master Gage assist his speed, a good dayes worke we ha made, To rescue Innocence so soone betrayd. For her supposed vertues, Royall Queene Looke on your sister with a smiling brow, And if her fault merite not too much hate, Let her be censur'd with all lenity, Let your deepe hatred end where it began, She hath binne too long banisht from the sun. We beare this mind, we errors would not feed, Nor cherish wrongs, nor yet see Innocents bleed. Myrror of vertue and bright natures pride, behind the arras. Pitty it had been, such beauty should haue dy'd
speeches.Eiz:: My honor'd Lord farewell, vnwilling I With griefe and woe must continue, Helpe me to some inke and paper good Sir Harry.
speeches.Cla:: Madame, not I, I neare slept soundlyer for the time. Neither Madame. Madame not I. A milking. Better be a Milk-maid free, then a Madame in bondage. Oh had'st thou heard the Princesse yesternight, Sitting within an arbor all alone to heare a Milk-mayd sing, It would haue moou'd a flynty hart to melt, Weeping and wishing, wishing and weeping, A thousand tymes she with her selfe debates, With the poore Milk-maid to exchange estates, Shee was a Sempster in the tower being a Princesse, And shall I her poore gentlewoman, disdayne To be a Milk-maid in the country. The Princesse gone, and I left here behind, Come, come our horses shall out-strip the wind. Yes master Gage, but heauie at the hart, For she was frited with a dreame this night. She said, she drempt her sister was new married, And sat vpon a high Emperiall throne, That she her selfe was cast into a dungeon, Where enemyes enuiron'd her about, Offering their weapons to her naked brest; Nay they would scarcly giue her leaue to pray, They made such hast to hurry her away. Then did I dreame of weddings, and of flowers, Me thought I was within the finest garden, That euer mortall eie did yet behould, Then strayght me thought some of the cheife were pickt To dresse the bride, O 'twas the rarest show, To see the bride goe smiling longst the streets, As if she went to happynes eternall.
speeches.Eliz: Did'st not thou put this booke into my hand? Then 'twas by inspiration, heauen I trust With his eternall hand, will guide the iust. What chapter's this? Who so putteth his trust in the Lord, Shall not be confounded: My sauiour thankes, on thee my hope I build, Thou lou'st poore Innocents, and art their shield.
speeches.Gres:: I pray your honor to regard my hast, My Lord you know his highnes treasure stayes, And cannot be transported this three months, Vnles that now your honor seale my warrant. How, the Princesse death? thankes heauen, By whome I am made a willing instrument her life to saue, That may liue crown'd when thou art in thy graue. My dutie to them all.
speeches.Phil:: Our Chancelor Lords, this is our sealing day, This our states busines; is our signet there? And may the heauens applaud this vnity, Accurst be they that first procur'd this wrong, Now by my crowne, you ha been kept downe too long. My soule is ioyfull that this peace is made, A peace that pleaseth heauen and earth, and all, Redeeming captiue thoughts from captiue thrall, Faire Queene, the serious busines of my father, Is now at hand to be accomplished, Of your faire sight needes must take my leaue, Returne I shall, tho parting cause vs greeue. Yet faire Queene hope the best I shall returne, VVho met with ioy, tho now sadly mourne.
speeches.Phyl:: Our sisters hart, Lo: Howard what meanes this?
speeches.Clow:: And Ile not be long after you, for I am sure My curtall will cary me as fast as your double Gelding. Come neighbor, come away, euery man his faggot, And his double pot, for ioy of the old Queenes death, Let bells ring, and children sing. For we may haue cause to remember, The seauenteenth day of Nouember. I, but do not you know the old prouerbe, VVe must liue by the quicke, and not by the dead.
speeches.Ben:: My Lord of Sussex I can tell ill newes, The Cardinall Poole that now was firmly well, Is sodenly falne sicke and like to die.
speeches.Karow:: God saue the Queene, God saue Elizabeth.
speeches.Karew:: My horse did you allegeance at the gate, For there he broke his necke, and there he lyes, For I my selfe had much a do to rise, The fall hath brus'd me, yet I liue to cry, God blesse your Grace, God blesse your maiesty. Thankes to your maiesty, happy be my tongue, That first breath'd right, to one that had such wrong.
speeches.Broc:: Am I preuented in my hast, O chance accurst! My hopes did sooth me, that I was the first; Let not my duty be ore swayd by spleene, Long liue my Soueraigne, and God saue the Queene.
Let's guard our Soueraigne praysing that power: That can throw downe and raise within an hower. Ex: omnes.
speeches.Brock:: I of your Guard. I Sargeant Trumpetor present my Mace.
speeches.Maior:: I from this Citty London do present, This Purse and Bible to your Maiesty, A thowsand of your faithfull Cittizens, In Veluet Coats and Chaines well mounted, stay To greet their royall Soueraigne on the way.
